response:
The creature is a sessile, colonial organism that looks less like an animal than a low, branching mineral thicket that has learned to breathe. Locals of the imagination might call it a **glassreed**.

It grows in shallow, mineral-rich basins under a dim orange star. A mature colony is about the height of a person and several meters across, made of translucent, amber tubes jointed like bamboo. The tubes are not plants and not glass; they are a living silicate–protein composite, stiff enough to stand in wind, flexible enough to flex when the ground shivers. Inside each tube, pale fluid moves in slow pulses. At the joints, fans of fine filaments open and close like eyelids.

It has no head, no face, and no central brain. Cognition, if the word fits, is distributed. Each tube is a module with its own simple nerve net; the colony shares signals through electrolyte films where tubes fuse. A sharp touch on one side makes the whole stand lean and seal; a chemical cue in the water can make every filament orient the same way. It is closer to a coral or a siphonophore than to a vertebrate: one body made of many semi-independent zooids, none of which can live long alone.

Its metabolism is split. The filaments harvest weak sunlight and also pull metal ions and dissolved silica from the brine, laying them down as new tube wall. Deeper in the stand, buried root-like stolons host symbiotic microbes that oxidize sulfur compounds seeping from the rock. The glassreed trades sugars and shelter for that chemical energy. In eclipse season, when the star is hidden for weeks, the colony goes nearly transparent and lives almost entirely on that chemosynthetic partnership, slowing its pulses until it seems dead.

It senses the world chemically and mechanically. The filaments taste gradients of salt, sulfur, and the waste of other organisms. Vibration sensors in the joints detect footfalls, rain, and the low-frequency calls of flying grazers. It has no eyes, but pigment patches along the tubes darken or clear in response to light, and neighboring colonies can “read” those patterns across a few meters of still air—crude, slow signaling, more like a blush than a language.

It does not hunt. Small swimming animals shelter in the tubes and are sometimes trapped when a joint pinches shut, but the glassreed mostly absorbs what they shed: mucus, dead skin, mineral dust. In return the stand breaks wind, concentrates nutrients, and keeps the basin from crusting over. It is an ecosystem engineer more than a predator.

Reproduction is twofold. Most growth is clonal: a stolon creeps through wet sediment and lifts a new tube. Once a decade, when sulfur vents surge and the brine warms, colonies release clouds of microscopic, armored propagules from pores at the tube tips. Those propagules drift, settle, and only fuse with unrelated colonies. Fusion is a negotiation. Incompatible chemistries cause the contact zone to scar and wall off; compatible ones merge circulatory films and share symbionts. A “forest” of glassreed is therefore a patchwork of clones and fused lineages, old partnerships visible as darker seams in the amber.

What kind of organism is it? Not a plant, though it photosynthesizes. Not an animal in the Earth sense, though it moves, senses, and sometimes traps prey. It is a colonial, mixotrophic, chemosymbiotic metazoan-like life form: modular, sessile, mineral-bodied, and dependent on microbial partners. If you had to file it somewhere familiar, the nearest drawer would read “reef-building animal that also behaves like a lichen”—a creature whose body is a habitat, and whose life is a slow argument with stone, light, and sulfur.

response:
The creature is a sessile, colonial organism the size of a small tree, known here as a **glassmound**. It lives on a cold, dim world where the atmosphere is dense and nitrogen-rich, and liquid water is scarce but brines collect in shallow stone basins.

From a distance it looks like a low mound of smoked crystal, two to three meters across and about a meter high, rooted in a mineral seep. Closer, the “glass” resolves into thousands of fused, translucent tubes, each no thicker than a finger, packed in a hexagonal lattice. The tubes are not mineral. They are living tissue stiffened by a silica-organic composite, grown slowly from dissolved minerals in the brine. Light passes through the walls and scatters inside, so the whole colony glows faintly green-gold even under a weak sun.

Each tube is an individual, but they share a common basal mat. The mat is a dense network of hollow filaments that move fluids, mineral ions, and signaling molecules between neighbors. A damaged tube is sealed off and its remaining resources are drawn back into the colony. New tubes bud from the mat’s rim, so the mound expands outward over decades rather than growing upward.

Its energy system is mixed. The tube walls host pigment layers that harvest the planet’s redder sunlight, but photosynthesis alone is not enough. The basal filaments also oxidize reduced minerals leaching from the rock—iron and sulfur compounds—extracting chemical energy the way some Earth microbes do at vents. By day the colony stores surplus energy as dense, oily droplets suspended in internal fluid. By night those droplets are broken down to keep the shared circulatory flow moving.

It does not eat in any animal sense. Dissolved organics and mineral ions enter through microscopic pores along the lower tubes, filtered by a mucus-like lining that the colony continuously secretes and reabsorbs. Particulates are rejected. The same lining sheds a thin film onto the surrounding rock, slowly etching it and widening the seep the colony depends on.

There is no brain and no nervous system of the animal kind. Coordination is chemical and hydraulic. Pressure waves travel through the shared fluid when temperature, brine chemistry, or light changes, and neighboring tubes alter pore opening, pigment density, and budding rate in response. The colony can “lean” over years: tubes on the shaded side stay short and heavily mineralized, while tubes facing the seep grow longer and more translucent. From outside this looks like purposeful behavior. It is growth biased by local conditions.

Reproduction is twofold. Most of the time the colony simply expands and occasionally splits when the basal mat thins across a crack in the stone, leaving two genetically identical mounds. Less often, during rare thaws when brine floods the basin, mature tubes release clouds of microscopic, armored propagules. These are not seeds in the plant sense and not spores of a fungus. Each is a tiny, self-contained packet: a silica shell, a droplet of stored oil, a few pigment cells, and a filament primordium. They drift in the flood, settle where mineral-rich water persists, and if conditions hold, grow a new mat. Most never do.

The closest Earth analogies are partial and imperfect: reef-building animals for the colonial, mineralized body; vent microbes for the chemical energy; desert plants for slow, resource-hoarding growth. It is none of those. It is a mineral-harvesting colony, photosynthetic at the margins, chemically fueled at the root, sessile, modular, and effectively immortal so long as the seep does not dry.

response:
The veldt-singer is a colonial animal that lives on the wind-scoured plains of a tidally locked world, always in the dim band where permanent day meets permanent night. From a distance it looks like a low, pale thicket of glass reeds that hum when the wind crosses them. Up close it is one organism: a crawling mat of fused individuals that never fully separate after budding.

Its body is a quilt of hexagonal plates, each about the width of a human hand, the color of dried bone with a faint violet sheen. The plates are not armor in the crustacean sense. They are living shells of mineralized protein, grown from the skin and laced with channels of blue-green fluid. That fluid is not blood as we know it. It carries dissolved metals and a photosymbiotic microbe that the creature farms inside itself. In the twilight, the microbes do not photosynthesize much. They instead run on weak infrared leaking from the hot dayside and on chemical energy the host pulls from iron-rich dust. The plates glow faintly when the colony is well fed, dimming when it is hungry.

There is no head. Feeding happens anywhere along the leading edge. The margin of the mat frays into hundreds of hollow, muscular tubules that probe the soil and the air. Some tubules drink groundwater heavy with dissolved salts. Others sweep airborne spores and grit into a grinding chamber just under the plates, where grains of rock are crushed and the organic film on them is digested. Waste minerals are excreted as a chalky trail, so a traveling colony leaves a pale ribbon behind it, visible from orbit as a slow scribble across the plain.

Movement is peristaltic. The whole mat tightens and loosens in waves, each plate tilting on a flexible joint so the colony creeps a few body-lengths an hour. It cannot sprint. It does not need to. Almost nothing on the plain can catch it, and almost nothing wants to. The plates taste bitter and are threaded with a mild neurotoxin meant for small burrowers, not for large predators. The real defense is the song.

Along the upper surface, certain plates have grown into hollow spines of different lengths. Wind across their openings produces tones, and the colony can flex the spines to retune them. The resulting chord is not language in a human sense, but it is coordinated. Neighboring colonies answer, and the pitch encodes rough information: mineral richness of the ground, the approach of a dust storm, the presence of a rotting carcass worth diverting toward. A lone mat sings thinly. A gathering of mats, fused temporarily along their edges to share fluid and microbes, can fill the twilight with a low organ-chord that carries for kilometers. After the exchange they often separate again, though sometimes two mats stay joined and become one larger individual. There is no fixed adult size. A colony can be a dinner plate or a field.

Reproduction is mostly by fragmentation. A well-fed mat pinches off a daughter patch, stocks it with symbiotic microbes, and lets the wind and its own slow crawl carry it away. Once in a long seasonal cycle, when the terminator storms pile nutrient dust in deep drifts, colonies also produce free-swimming gametes in shallow melt pools at the edge of the ice. Those gametes are the only truly mobile, individual phase: tiny, ciliated, short-lived, and incapable of feeding. They fuse, settle, and grow a first plate. Everything after that is colonial.

It is an animal in the broad sense—it moves, it ingests, it has muscle and a nervous net—but its nervous system is a mesh with no central brain, more like a jellyfish than a vertebrate. Memory, such as it is, lives in the pattern of which plates are thickened and which tubules are primed. Cut the mat in half and both halves remember the song they were singing, imperfectly, and both will try to finish it.

Seen at dusk, a veldt-singer is easy to mistake for weather: a pale shimmer, a chord in the wind, a chalk line on the ground. It is a grazer of dust and dissolved metal, a herd that is also a single body, and a singer whose voice is an organ as much as a behavior.

response:
**Vesperil, the glass-veined grazer of the dusk plains**

Imagine a low, six-limbed animal about the size of a large dog, built for a world with a dim orange sun, thin air, and soil rich in metals. Locals might call it a vesperil. It is not a plant, a fungus, or an Earth animal, though pieces of its body recall all three.

### Shape and surface
Its body is a flattened oval, low to the ground, with a flexible central keel rather than a rigid backbone. Six jointed limbs radiode out: the front pair ends in scooping pads used for digging and feeding, the middle pair is longer and used for walking, and the rear pair can lock into the soil as anchors when wind rises. There is no distinct head. Sensory tissue forms a horseshoe of dark pits along the leading edge.

The hide is not scales or fur. It is a living mosaic of mineral plates grown from silica and iron compounds the animal extracts from the soil, set in a leathery matrix. Between the plates run translucent “glass veins”—channels of clear tissue that conduct light inward. In shade the animal looks charcoal and rust-colored. In low sun the veins glow dull amber as light reaches the photosynthetic symbionts under the plates.

### How it makes a living
The vesperil is a **chemo-photo mixotroph with internal symbionts**, not a pure hunter or a pure plant-eater.

- It grazes mineral crusts and microbial mats, scraping them up with the front pads and grinding them in a muscular gizzard lined with sand it swallows and renews.
- Dissolved metals and sulfur compounds feed colonies of bacteria housed in a spongy organ along the belly. Those bacteria oxidize the compounds and release energy the host can use, much as tube worms rely on vent bacteria, though the setting here is open plain rather than a deep-sea vent.
- The glass veins and thin windows in the plates let weak sunlight reach a second set of symbionts that fix carbon when the sky is clear. On long cloudy stretches the animal leans harder on chemistry and stored fats; on bright days it can rest and “charge.”

So biologically it sits between an animal host and a walking lichen: a mobile body that cannot live long if its microbial partners die, and microbes that cannot disperse well without the host.

### Sensing and behavior
It has no eyes in the Earth sense. The leading pits detect polarized light, temperature gradients, and the faint electrical fields of wet soil. A ring of pressure-sensitive hairs along the limb joints reads wind and footfall. Communication is chemical and vibrational: individuals leave metallic-smelling trails and drum the ground with a hind limb when a storm front or a burrowing predator is near. They do not form herds so much as loose feeding lines that drift with the richest crusts.

When threatened it does not run far. It drops, locks the rear limbs, and floods the outer plates with a bitter metal-rich fluid that hardens into a temporary crust. Predators that bite get a mouthful of abrasive mineral and an unpleasant dose of oxidized sulfur compounds. The animal then inches toward a rock seam and wedges itself in until the threat passes.

### Internal plan
Circulation is an open bath of copper-based fluid, blue-green when oxygenated, moved by a series of muscular pumps rather than one heart. Gas exchange happens across thin folds under the rear limb joints, kept moist by a wax that slows water loss in the thin air. Nitrogen waste is recycled into the symbiont organs instead of being dumped, which matters on a planet where usable nitrogen is patchy.

There are three sexes, not two. Two produce different kinds of gametes; the third is a “carrier” that incubates the fused cell in a pouch and later plants a resistant cyst in mineral soil. The cyst can sit dormant through a dust season, then crack open into a soft juvenile that must acquire the right bacteria from the crust within its first few days or starve. That dependency is the clearest clue to what kind of organism it is: a holobiont, an individual only in partnership.

### What it is, in plain terms
A vesperil is a slow, armored, six-limbed grazer whose energy comes from sunlight and from metal- and sulfur-eating microbes it farms inside its body. It senses the world mostly by light polarization, chemistry, and vibration; it reproduces through a three-party cycle and a dormant soil cyst; and it defends itself by becoming, briefly, more rock than animal.

Nothing about it is meant as a real species or a buildable organism—only a coherent picture of how life might look if mineral chemistry and dim light mattered as much as flesh and blood.

response:
**Virellid of the glassflats (Thalassomere vitrifer)**

On a cold, tidally locked world whose nightside is locked under a perpetual ice ocean and whose dayside is a shallow, sun-scorched sea, the narrow twilight belt is a band of permanent fog and black basalt shallows. There the virellid lives: a slow, colonial animal-plant that looks less like a beast than like a walking greenhouse.

### Form
A mature individual is about the size of a draft horse and shaped like a low, segmented raft. Six jointed, translucent legs splay from a cartilaginous keel. The body is not solid flesh so much as a lattice of glassy plates—mineralized chitin shot through with silica—forming a double row of arched chambers. Inside those chambers float amber and green sacs the size of fists. In still air the creature seems carved from wet glass; when it moves, light fractures across the plates and the sacs pulse.

A blunt, hooded head sits low at the front. It has no eyes. Instead, a fan of pale, hair-fine filaments bristles from the hood’s rim, and two lateral “lanterns”—fluid-filled blisters—glow a dim blue-green when the animal is alarmed or courting. The mouth is a ventral slit lined with rasping, replaceable plates, not teeth. At the rear, a skirt of frilled tissue trails in the water like wet silk.

It is neither fully aquatic nor terrestrial. The legs are for wading; the body rides half-submerged. On land it is clumsy. In water deeper than its keel it cannot swim, only drift.

### What kind of organism it is
It is an animal in the broad sense: it moves, has a nervous system, and must take in complex carbon from outside. But it is also a walking symbiosis. The amber sacs are not organs of the virellid alone. They are sealed gardens of photosynthetic microbes the animal inherits from its parent and cultivates for life. The green sacs are a second partner: sulfur- and iron-cycling bacteria that let it mine energy from the mineral-rich seep water of the twilight shallows.

So the virellid is a **chemo-photosynthetic holobiont**—an animal whose metabolism is incomplete without its internal microbiome. Alone, its own tissues can only ferment. With the sacs intact, it can live for weeks on light filtered through fog plus dissolved minerals, and only occasionally needs to graze.

### Internal biology
- **Circulation.** There is no closed blood system. A slow hemolymph, thick with copper-bearing pigments, moves by the contraction of the plate lattice itself. Each step pumps fluid forward; each rest lets it settle. Oxygen is not the main electron acceptor. The twilight sea is oxygen-poor. Instead, the animal’s tissues hand electrons to the bacterial sacs, which dump them onto sulfate and ferric iron in the water it continually sips through gill-slits under the keel.
- **Skeleton.** The glassy plates are grown, not secreted once and forgotten. Specialized cells lay down silica spicules inside a protein matrix, then mineralize them with a thin carbonate glaze. Cracks heal. Lost plates regrow over months. The plates also act as lenses: they concentrate the weak red light of the permanent sunset onto the photosynthetic sacs.
- **Nerves.** A ladder of ganglia runs the length of the keel, with a larger hood ganglion that integrates chemical and mechanical sense. There is no central “brain” capable of the kind of modeling a vertebrate does. Memory is short and local—each leg pair remembers the last safe footing better than the head does.
- **Senses.** Smell and taste are primary. The filament fan samples dissolved metals, microbial metabolites, and the chemical wake of other virellids. Vibration sensors in the leg joints read the slap of waves and the footfalls of scavengers. The lantern blisters are not eyes; they are signaling organs, and also crude light meters. True vision is absent. On this world, fog and low light made eyes a poor investment.
- **Temperature.** It is cold-blooded in the strict sense, but the bacterial sacs run slightly warm. A resting virellid in 4 °C water may hold its chamber fluid near 9 °C. That gradient is precious. If the sacs die, the animal chills, slows, and usually starves within days.

### Feeding and ecology
Most of its energy is “eaten” as light and minerals. The mouth is for supplements and emergencies: films of microbial mat, shed exoskeletons, the soft tissues of dead animals washed into the shallows. It does not hunt. It will, however, stand over a fresh carcass and let its frilled skirt secrete enzymes that loosen tissue, then sip the slurry. Locals of any expedition would call that scavenging, not predation.

It shapes its habitat. By wading the same paths for years, colonies cut channels that keep mineral-rich seep water moving. Other small animals shelter under the glassy belly. When a virellid dies, the plates do not rot quickly; they become reefs for the mats it once grazed.

### Life cycle
Reproduction is slow and public. Adults are simultaneous hermaphrodites but rarely self-fertilize; chemical kinship markers make close relatives taste “wrong.” Two animals face each other in knee-deep water, lanterns bright, and press hoods together for hours. Each passes a packet of gametes into a temporary brood pocket under the other’s keel. Fertilized embryos ride there for a season, each already seeded with a bead of parental microbes squeezed from the sacs.

Juveniles drop as coin-sized, legless discs. They drift until they lodge against a mineral seep, grow a first pair of legs, and only then begin to plate. A full adult takes roughly fifteen local years. Colonies are loose: individuals keep a body-length apart, oriented so their skirts do not tangle, and share chemical alarm. There is no hive mind and no hierarchy beyond “the one currently blocking the seep moves or is climbed over.”

### Behavior you would actually notice
A healthy virellid is almost still. It shifts a leg every few minutes. The sacs brighten when a break in the fog lets red light through, and dim when a squall passes. If startled—by a heavy footfall, or by the sour chemistry of a decaying rival—it does not flee fast. It locks its plates, vents a cloud of metallic, iodine-smelling fluid from the gill-slits, and lowers its body until the keel kisses the rock. The fluid is not a weapon. It is a concentrated waste brine that confuses chemical hunters and makes the animal taste foul.

Courtship is the only time it is beautiful in motion: lanterns strobing in a slow alternating pattern, skirts lifting, plates clicking once as the brood pockets open.

### What it is not
It is not a vertebrate, not an insect, not a plant that learned to walk. The nearest Earth analogy is a brachiopod or horseshoe-crab body plan married to a lichen’s dependence on partners, then scaled up and taught to farm light through its own skeleton. Its “kind” is colonial, modular, and metabolically incomplete: an organism whose identity is the partnership, not the glassy animal alone.

If you cut out the sacs and left the animal breathing in rich air, it would not become a normal beast. It would become a slowly failing fermenter, blind, cold, and finished. The glass, the legs, and the glow are only the visible half of the creature. The rest is a garden it carries, and cannot live without.

The **vellid** is a slow, colonial grazer of the high plateaus on a cold, dim world with thick carbon-dioxide air and orange-red light from a long-lived star. From a distance it looks like a low cairn of wet slate that has begun to crawl.

**Form.** An adult colony is about two meters across and knee-high, built of six to twelve overlapping plates of dark mineralized tissue. The plates are not a shell in the vertebrate sense; they are living armor, thick with iron and silica, perforated by thousands of fine pores. Between the plates a pale, translucent mantle sometimes wells out and touches the ground. That mantle is the animal’s only soft surface, and it is sticky with a thin film of gel. There is no head, no eyes, and no mouth you could point to. A ring of short, stiff bristles around the mantle’s rim is the closest thing to a face: each bristle is a hollow tube lined with cells that taste dissolved minerals and the faint chemical wake of other vellids.

**How it lives.** The vellid does not eat other creatures in any familiar way. Its plates host a dense skin of photosynthetic microbes that thrive in the weak red light, and the colony itself supplies them with water and trace metals scraped from the rock. In return the microbes leak sugars into a shared internal fluid. On the shaded underside, a different set of microbes ferments whatever organic film the mantle has mopped up—pollen-like spores, dead microbial mats, the occasional soft carcass. The vellid is therefore a composite organism: a mineral-armored host whose energy budget is mostly rented from its symbionts. Cut the plates away from the light for too long and the colony starves even if the ground is rich.

Movement is almost geological. The mantle inches forward by a coordinated squeeze of fluid-filled chambers, like a very slow slug, and the plates ratchet after it. A healthy colony covers a few body-lengths in a day. When the wind rises it stops, clamps down, and lets dust scour the plates clean so the microbes can photosynthesize again.

**Senses and behavior.** Without eyes, it reads the world chemically and mechanically. Vibrations in the rock tell it when a larger scavenger is near; a sudden change in carbon dioxide or a bitter peptide in the film tells it that another colony has claimed the patch. Colonies of the same lineage merge plates at the edges and share fluid for a season, then split again. Unrelated colonies do not fight. They simply stop, turn, and leave a bare strip of stone between them, as if the ground itself had drawn a boundary.

**Life cycle.** Reproduction is a slow budding. After several local years a colony extrudes a small, unarmored nodule from the mantle’s rim, packs it with a starter set of both microbial partners, and abandons it on a sunlit ledge. The nodule mineralizes its first plate within weeks. There are no sexes and no pairing. Genetic mixing happens rarely, when two colonies briefly fuse and exchange a few host cells before parting. Most of the time a vellid’s “children” are near-clones, distinguished mainly by which microbial strains they happened to inherit.

**What kind of organism it is.** It is not a plant, though it photosynthesizes by proxy, and not an animal in the strict Earth sense, though it moves, tastes, and avoids threats. The closest honest description is a colonial, chemosensory grazer whose body is a living greenhouse: mineral armor outside, a shared circulatory gel inside, and an obligate partnership with microbes that do most of the metabolic work. Individually a plate is almost inert. Together, plates, mantle, and microbes are one organism—slow, local, and entirely of that dim plateau.

**Virelune, the glass-lung wanderer**

On the twilight plains of Kethra-4, under a dim orange star and a sky the color of bruised copper, lives the virelune. It is roughly the size of a small horse, but nothing about its silhouette suggests a mammal. Picture a low, six-limbed body the color of wet slate, with a translucent crest like frozen smoke running from the nape to the tail.

### Form
The body is a flattened oval, about two meters long, held barely a hand’s breadth off the ground. Six jointed legs radiate from the sides. The front pair are longer and end in three soft, hook-tipped digits used for probing crevices. The middle pair carry most of the weight. The hind pair are shorter and denser, built for sudden reverse springs when the animal needs to bolt backward into a burrow.

There is no distinct head. At the forward rim sits a ring of seven dark eye-pits, each a cup of black pigment under a clear mineralized lens. They do not swivel; the creature turns the whole body to change its view. Between the eyes, a slit mouth opens sideways, lined with flexible keratin-like plates rather than teeth. It does not chew. It scrapes, then swallows.

A sail of living glass rises along the back. It is not glass, but a lattice of silica spicules grown into a thin, honeycombed crest, sheathed in a film so clear that the internal vessels show as faint silver threads. The crest catches the weak starlight and the planet’s frequent auroras. Locals—if there were any—would see it glow faintly blue-green at dusk.

### Skin and skeleton
The outer hide is a tough, slightly flexible cuticle embedded with microscopic silica grains, so it rasps like fine sandpaper. Under that is a layer of pale, almost gelatinous tissue that stores water and salts. The “bones” are not calcium. They are hollow rods of chitin-silica composite, light and springy, jointed with pads of elastic protein. Break one and it splinters into glittering fibers, not shards of white bone.

### How it lives
Kethra-4’s air is thin and rich in carbon dioxide, with traces of hydrogen sulfide near the ground. The virelune does not have lungs in the earthly sense. The crest is a gas-exchange organ: a vast surface of tiny chambers where dissolved gases move across a moist membrane into a circulating fluid. That fluid is not red. It is a milky blue, colored by a copper-bearing pigment that binds oxygen poorly but handles the local mix of gases well enough. In still air the crest flares; in wind it folds flat so the animal is not torn off its feet.

It feeds on the mineral-crusted microbial mats that coat the plains—sheets of bacteria and algae-like cells that photosynthesize in the orange light and fix sulfur from the soil. The mouth plates rasp the mat into a slurry. A muscular crop grinds it with ingested sand. Farther back, a long gut hosts symbiotic microbes that strip energy from the sulfur compounds and the tough polysaccharides in the mat. The animal itself contributes little more than the grinding and the steady walk. Much of its nutrition is borrowed from those internal partners.

Water is scarce. The virelune drinks dew that condenses on its own crest at night, channeling droplets down grooves into the mouth. It also extracts moisture from the mats. Excess salts are excreted as a chalky crust along the leg joints, which it scrapes off against rocks.

### Senses and behavior
Vision is tuned to the orange-red and to ultraviolet glints off wet mineral films, so food patches look brighter than bare stone. It has no ears. Vibration sensors in the leg pads feel the footfalls of the larger burrowers that share the plain, and a chemical sense in the mouth slit reads the sulfur gradient of fresh mats.

Virelunes are solitary except during the brief wet season, when standing pools form in old impact craters. Then they gather, crest to crest, and exchange packets of gut symbionts by mouth-to-mouth contact—a messy, necessary sharing that keeps each animal’s internal community diverse. Eggs, if they can be called that, are leathery capsules buried in warm ash. There is no parental care. Hatchlings emerge already six-legged and crestless; the sail grows over the first two local years as silica accumulates from the diet.

They are not predators and not prey in any dramatic sense. Their main danger is desiccation and the occasional collapse of a mat field after a sulfur vent dies. When threatened, a virelune does not flee forward. It springs backward on the hind legs, crest folded, and wedges itself into the nearest rock cleft, presenting only the abrasive flank.

### What kind of organism it is
In earthly terms it is neither animal nor plant nor fungus, though it occupies the niche of a slow grazer. Call it an animal-like heterotroph: a motile, multicellular creature with specialized tissues, a gut, and a nervous net concentrated in a forward ring rather than a brain. Its energy comes from food, not from its own photosynthesis, even though the crest glows. The glow is waste chemistry and trapped light, not a solar panel. Its skeleton is silica-reinforced, its oxygen carrier copper-based, its digestion largely outsourced to symbionts. Under it lies a living layer of symbiotic microbes—filamentous, oxygen-tolerant chemotrophs that the vaelith cultivates rather than digests. They oxidize reduced sulfur and iron compounds scraped from the rocks and leak usable energy compounds into the host’s circulation. The cuticle itself hosts a second partnership: flattened pigment cells that capture the weak red-orange light of Kessara’s star and pass electrons inward. The vaelith is therefore a mixotroph. Its “kind” is a slow, glass-armored film-grazer of a metal-rich, oxygen-poor world — built to read wind and ground-shake, to drink chemistry from the dust, and to leave a translucent skeleton when the soft life inside finally goes still.

The Siltbell is a slow, translucent organism that lives in the shallow tidal shelves of a dim, ammonia-rich world. Embedded in that gel are thousands of small, repeating modules—each a cluster of cells around a fluid-filled sac. Some modules pump; some store minerals; some hold symbiotic microbes. Inside those modules live dense colonies of microbes that crack complex molecules the Siltbell cannot process alone. In return, the host keeps them warm, wet, and supplied with trace metals. Much of the Siltbell’s energy comes from this partnership, supplemented by faint photosynthetic pigments in the upper gel that catch the weak red light of its star. In deeper water, where light fails, individuals grow paler and rely almost entirely on the microbes and on chemical gradients seeping from the sediment.

What looks like breathing is a slow pulse. The dome swells and settles every few minutes, drawing ammonia-rich water through pores and expelling waste fluid through others. It has no lungs and no blood. Dissolved gases and nutrients move through the gel by diffusion, helped by the pumping modules. It senses the world through chemistry and pressure more than sight. Pigment patches on the dome detect changes in light and cast a dull inner glow when the animal is disturbed, which neighboring Siltbells can see through the murk. The filament fringe tastes the water for salts, toxins, and the chemical signature of other Siltbells. A ripple in the silt is felt as a traveling wave through the gel. There are no eyes, ears, or nose—only surfaces that report what touches them.

A settled Siltbell may live for decades, growing wider rather than taller, until storm-scour or a chemical seep kills the microbial partners and the gel clouds, collapses, and becomes part of the silt.

response:
**Name:** the glass-backed stalker (*Luminovita umbracollis*, as a xenobiologist might file it)

**World:** a tidally locked moon with a thin, sulfur-scented atmosphere, dim red-star light, and a surface broken into basalt shelves, iron-oxide dust, and shallow alkaline pools. Day never truly ends; the “night” side is only a long twilight. The stalker lives in the terminator zone, where light is low and fog hangs over the pools.

### Body plan
It is about the size of a large dog, low and elongated, roughly 1.4 meters from snout to tail tip. It is not a vertebrate. Its body is built on a radial-bilateral hybrid: a firm central keel of mineralized cartilage runs the length of the torso, with six jointed limbs arranged in three pairs. The front pair is longer and ends in hooked, keratin-like claws used for climbing wet rock. The middle pair is broader, paddle-flat, and used for swimming and bracing. The rear pair is short and powerful, used for bursts of speed on land.

The skin is a tight mosaic of translucent plates over a dark, almost black dermis. Along the back, those plates are especially clear—hence “glass-backed.” Under them sits a sheet of symbiotic microbes that glow a dull copper-green when the animal is alarmed or courting. The glow is not decoration only; it is a signal and a waste-heat dump. The microbes oxidize sulfur compounds the animal cannot fully process, and the light is a byproduct.

### How it senses the world
There are no eyes in the familiar sense. A band of pigment-cups runs along both flanks and over the crown. Each cup holds a small lens of crystallized protein and a layer of cells sensitive to near-infrared and to the faint red of the parent star. Together they give a wide, low-resolution panorama rather than a focused image. It “sees” heat edges and moving silhouettes better than fine detail.

Along the snout are two rows of hollow spines. These are chemoreceptors. Air and water both pass over them; dissolved metals, ammonia, and the sour smell of rotting microbial mats tell it where food and rivals are. A low, drum-like organ under the keel picks up vibration through rock and water. It hunts as much by footfall as by sight.

### Feeding
It is an ambush omnivore with a strong bias toward animal prey. The mouth is a vertical slit that can open into a triangular gape. Inside is not a tongue but a muscular bulb that everts, coats prey in a sticky mucus, and reels it in. The mucus contains enzymes that begin digestion outside the body—useful on cold, slow-metabolizing prey.

Its usual targets are palm-sized crustacean analogues that graze the pool margins, and soft-bodied burrowers that surface at “dusk” (the dimmer hours when fog thickens). It will also scrape microbial mats and swallow mineral-rich mud when prey is scarce. A gut pouch hosts a second set of symbionts that crack sulfur and iron compounds, so a meal of mud is not empty calories; it is a slow mineral harvest.

### Internal life
Circulation is open-ish: a contractile dorsal vessel pushes a copper-based hemolymph through sinuses rather than a closed capillary net. The blood is pale blue-green when oxygenated and muddy gray when spent. Oxygen uptake happens through the skin plates and through a pair of book-like internal gills that stay moist even on land, folded into chambers that open just behind the middle limbs. On a long stalk across dry shelves it must pause at pools or it begins to suffocate.

It does not maintain a high body temperature. Metabolism is slow except during a chase, when stored high-energy sulfur compounds are burned in a short anaerobic burst. Afterward it lies still for a long time, plates flushed dark as blood is shunted to the gill chambers.

Waste nitrogen leaves mostly as uric-acid crystals voided with the mucus of the occasional “spit-shed,” a behavior that also clears fouled mouth enzymes. Water is precious; the plates and a waxy surface film cut evaporation.

### Reproduction and life cycle
Sexes are not fixed for life. Each adult carries both egg and sperm tissues, but only one set is active in a given season, cued by pool chemistry and the length of the fog cycle. Two stalkers meet on a flat rock, align keel to keel, and exchange packets through a temporary pore near the tail base. There is no prolonged pairing.

Eggs are laid in strings under the lip of a pool, glued with the same mucus used in feeding, now reformulated to harden in alkaline water. A parent—whichever one last carried the active egg tissue—guards the string for several local weeks, flashing its back-glow if a rival approaches. Hatchlings are miniature, six-limbed, and fully aquatic for their first year, breathing only by gill. The glass plates thicken as they shift to amphibious life. A full lifespan, if it avoids larger shoreline predators and pool-drying events, is on the order of fifteen to twenty local years.

### Behavior
It is solitary and territorial about a few pools and the rock between them. Threat displays are a raised keel, a full copper-green backlight, and a rasping sound made by rubbing the hollow snout spines together. It rarely fights; the claws are for grip and for pinning small prey, not for duels. Most conflicts end when one animal dims its glow and slips into the water.

At rest it presses flat, plates matching the basalt, microbes dimmed to near-black. From a distance it looks like a wet stone with a faint seam of light along one edge.

### What kind of organism it is
In Earth terms it is none of the familiar phyla, but the nearest analogies are a blend: the limb layout and open circulation suggest an arthropod-like animal; the external pre-digestion and book gills recall some chelicerates; the sulfur symbionts are more like what we see in deep-sea vent fauna. It is a cold-blooded, amphibious, microbe-dependent ambush predator, built for a dim, metal-rich, water-scarce shoreline rather than for a green, sunlit world.

response:
**The silt-mirror of Veyr is a slow, colonial animal that lives where an iron-rich mudflat meets a shallow ammonia sea.** Locals of the survey teams call it a silt-mirror; its own species name in the field notes is *Laminara umbra*.

It is not a single body. A mature silt-mirror is a quilt of hundreds to thousands of flat, palm-sized plates fused along their edges into a sheet that can cover a hectare of tidal flat. From a skiff it looks like wet slate with a faint bronze sheen. Walk close and the sheet is alive: each plate is a translucent, cartilage-like disk about 12–18 cm across and 2 cm thick, veined with dark branching channels. Between plates, the joints are soft and pearly, able to flex as the mud heaves.

### Body plan
Each plate is a module, not an organ. It has no head, no limbs, and no gut in the animal sense. The upper surface is a living mirror: a lattice of guanine-like crystals in a gel matrix that reflects the sky so well that birds—and survey drones—often miss the colony until they are standing on it. Under that skin is a thin photosynthetic layer, then a spongy mesoglea, then a lower surface carpeted in millions of hair-fine filaments that drink the mud.

The plates share three fluids through the seams:

- A blue circulatory gel that carries dissolved metals and waste.
- A slower amber gel that stores energy as long-chain sulfur-carbon compounds.
- A neural film, only a few cells thick, that spreads across the whole colony like a single shallow brain.

There is no central nervous system. Decisions are local and then average out. Touch one plate and a ripple of dimming runs outward at about a walking pace; the mirror dulls, then returns.

### How it lives
Veyr’s sun is dim and red. The silt-mirror does not rely on light alone. Its lower filaments host symbiotic microbes that oxidize iron and sulfide in the mud, the way tube-worm bacteria do on Earth’s vents, and pass sugars and metal-organic compounds upward. The photosynthetic skin is a supplement for the long polar days, not the main meal. In chemical terms it is a chemoautotroph with a light-harvesting side job: an animal-shaped mat that eats rust and rotten-egg chemistry and only snacks on photons.

It does not hunt. It filters. Suspended mineral dust, bacterial floc, and the occasional drifting larval crustacean are trapped in mucus on the mirror face and slowly drawn down microscopic pores into the mesoglea, where enzymes and symbionts break them apart. Large animals that settle on it are not eaten. They are discouraged. The skin can dump a burst of mildly alkaline, metal-rich mucus that stings soft tissue and crusts on chitin. After a few minutes the crust flakes off and the mirror is clean again.

### Senses and behavior
The neural film senses three things well: chemical gradients in the mud, pressure from footsteps or waves, and the angle of skylight on the crystal lattice. It has no eyes. Colonies still track the slow arc of the sun by how the mirror’s reflectance changes, and they tilt plates a few degrees by swelling one side of each joint. At midday the sheet is flatter and brighter; at dusk it buckles into low ridges that shed wind-blown grit.

When a storm is coming—signaled by a drop in dissolved oxygen and a metallic taste in the pore water—the colony does something that looks like thought. Plates along the seaward edge loosen their seams, curl, and sink a hand’s depth into the mud, anchoring the sheet. Inland plates pile slightly, forming a low berm. It is not intelligence in the vertebrate sense. It is a chemical habit refined over a very long time. Cut the neural film and the berm still forms, just slower and sloppier, because neighboring plates can still read the same water.

### Reproduction and growth
Silt-mirrors do not mate in pairs. Once a colony covers enough ground and its amber gel is fat with stored sulfur-carbon chains, hundreds of plates simultaneously grow a clear blister on their upper face. Inside each blister a few dozen tiny plate-buds form, each already seeded with a packet of the parental symbionts. On a spring tide the blisters rupture together. The buds are neutrally buoyant for a few hours, glittering like fish scales, and drift until they taste a mudflat with the right iron-to-sulfide ratio. Then they settle, grow filaments, and begin to fuse with any neighbor whose surface chemistry matches. Unrelated colonies can merge if their symbiont strains are compatible; incompatible ones keep a permanent seam and slowly push apart, which is why some flats look tiled by invisible borders.

A single plate can live for decades. A colony can persist for centuries, shedding and replacing modules the way a reef replaces coral heads. Dead plates do not rot quickly. Their crystal lattices and cartilage scaffolds settle into the mud and become the glittering shale that gives the tidal flats their name.

### What kind of organism it is
If you had to file it under a familiar kingdom, you would fail, and that is the point. It is closest to a colonial animal built like a hybrid of coral, jellyfish, and microbial mat:

- Modular and sessile, like a coral.
- Gel-bodied and net-nerved, like a cnidarian.
- Nutritionally dependent on internal chemoautotrophic microbes, like a vent tubeworm.
- Photosynthetic only as a backup, so not a plant and not a lichen.

It has tissues, a shared circulatory gel, coordinated behavior, and a life cycle with a dispersing larval stage, which is enough to call it an animal in the broad functional sense: a multicellular heterotroph-turned-chemotroph that moves energy through a body rather than through a mycelium or a mat alone. It does not have bones, a through-gut, or a brain. Its “skeleton” is the crystal mirror; its “stomach” is a garden of microbes; its “mind” is a film.

Stand on a silt-mirror at dusk and it will dim under your boots in a widening circle, tilt its plates to spill grit off your soles, and otherwise ignore you. By morning the circle is gone, the mirror is bright, and the only sign you were there is a faint alkaline crust that the next tide will take.

The creature is the glass-lung reedwalker, a slow, solitary animal that lives in the permanent twilight of a fog world. From a distance it looks less like an animal than like a stand of pale reeds that has decided to walk.

It stands about two and a half meters tall when fully extended. Its body is a narrow column of translucent tissue, the color of wet bone, supported by a flexible internal lattice of mineralized cartilage rather than a true skeleton. Six limbs branch from a jointed collar halfway up the trunk. Each limb is jointless in the vertebrate sense: a tapering tube of hydrostatic muscle, ridged with rings of stiff protein, that can lock or soften along its length. The tips split into three flattened hooks used for gripping stems, not for tearing flesh.

At the top of the column is not a head so much as a crown. A ring of eight hollow siphons opens outward, each lined with a dark fringe of chemoreceptive hairs. There are no eyes. Light on this planet is dim, red, and unreliable under the fog, so the reedwalker maps its world by taste and pressure. The siphons sample the air continuously. Fine threads of mucus inside them bind airborne molecules, and a slow peristaltic pulse carries those threads down into a central nerve knot the size of a fist. That knot is the animal’s only concentrated nervous tissue. Everything else is a distributed net of signal fibers running just under the skin, so a touch anywhere on the body is felt almost at once, but there is no brain that could be called a mind in any human sense—only a patient chemistry of approach and retreat.

The most striking organ is the lung. Down the front of the trunk runs a vertical slit that never fully closes. Behind it, a stack of glassy sacs hangs in the body cavity, each no thicker than a leaf and filled with a clear, slightly viscous fluid. The fluid is not water. It holds a dissolved metal salt that the creature gathers from mineral seeps, and that salt changes color as it binds gases. When the reedwalker is resting, the sacs are pale gold. When it has been feeding on the sulfurous mist that pools in low ground at dusk, they darken to green-black. The sacs are both respiratory organs and a slow energy store: the bound gases are later released into a second chamber where symbiotic microbes oxidize them, warming the body a few degrees above the fog. The creature does not breathe in pulses. A continuous draft moves through the slit, driven by the same rings of muscle that stiffen the trunk. In still air you can hear it—a soft, wet ticking, like condensation falling inside a pipe.

Its skin is the other half of its disguise. The outer layer is a living cuticle of interlocking silica scales, cloudy and slightly iridescent, grown from the same mineral budget as the lung salts. Between the scales, pores weep a thin film that beads the fog into droplets and runs them down to a gutter at the base of the trunk. The animal drinks almost nothing by mouth. Water, and the sparse organic dust trapped in it, are taken up through that film and through a mat of rootlike filaments that uncoil from the foot when it stands still. Those filaments are not roots in any plant sense. They are reversible. After an hour or a day, they withdraw into slits around the base, leaving a pale ring in the mud.

The reedwalker is not a plant, though it spends most of its life acting like one. It is an animal with a dual metabolism. While it stands, the microbes in its lung and gut ferment whatever organic haze and fallen spores the fog delivers, and the silica skin harvests a little energy from a dull photopigment that works in deep red light—too little to live on, enough to idle. When the fog thins and the chemical wind shifts, it walks. Movement is a slow toppling: one limb plants, the trunk leans, the base lifts, and the whole column advances half a meter. It can cover a few kilometers in a night if a rich seep lies upwind. It does not hunt. It grazes on the exudates of sessile fog-polyps and on the mineral crusts those polyps leave behind, scraping them with the hook-tips and tucking the scrapings into a ventral groove that leads to a simple gut. The gut is a straight tube with three chambers. The first kneads and dissolves. The second is a dark culture of the same metal-tolerant microbes. It has no sex in any familiar way, and no seasons that match a year. When two reedwalkers meet in a seep, they do not fight and they do not court. They stand close enough that their siphon crowns overlap, and for several hours they exchange strands of mucus loaded with packets of cells. Each packet is a copy of part of the donor’s microbial guild and a few of its own stem-cells, wrapped in a mineral shell. The recipient sorts them. Useful strains are kept. The rest are digested. It is not a plant, animal, or fungus in Earth terms, though parts of its life resemble all three. It is a **chemolithotrophic colonial eukaryote**: many genetically related modules share one circulatory gel and one reproductive core, while also hosting mineral-oxidizing microbes. Ecologically it functions as a slow grazer and scavenger of metal-rich films and dead organic mats, not a hunter.

### Body plan and tissues
- **Modules, not organs in the vertebrate sense.** Each lobe is a semi-independent unit with its own nerve net, but all lobes share a common hydrostatic gel. Cut one lobe away and it can crawl a short distance, then dies unless it re-fuses with the colony.
- **Skeleton.** No bones. Support comes from turgor in gel-filled chambers and a flexible lattice of silica-protein spicules, closer to a sponge’s scaffolding than to a shell.
- **Circulation.** A slow, non-pulsatile flow of copper-binding fluid moves nutrients and oxygen-analogue gases. The fluid is green-black and smells faintly of wet stone if spilled.
- **Nervous system.** A distributed net with a denser ring around the light vesicle. It can learn simple routes and remember mineral patches for days, but it has no single brain and no evidence of self-awareness in the human sense.
- **Skin.** A living biofilm of the host’s own cells plus symbionts. It exchanges gases directly and secretes a thin mucus that prevents desiccation in dry winds and poisons competing mats.

Sunlight barely reaches its habitat, so photosynthesis is minor. The virellid’s main energy comes from:
1. **Chemosynthesis by symbionts** that oxidize iron and sulfur compounds seeping from rock.
2. **External digestion.** Siphons lay down enzymes on microbial crusts and soft detritus, then suck up the broth. It does not bite or swallow chunks.
3. **A small light harvest.** The vesicle’s glow is mostly waste light from microbial metabolism; a few host pigments recapture a fraction of it. That makes the glow metabolically cheap rather than a costly display.

It grows slowly. A well-fed colony might add a new lobe every few local months.

Chemical pits taste metal ions, ammonia-like wastes, and the mucus of other virellids. Vibration-sensitive spicules detect footfalls and rockfalls. **The kel-warden (Thaumosiphon crystallum)** is a sessile, colonial organism of the twilight shelves of Veyra’s ice-locked moon, Thalass, where a subsurface ocean meets pale basalt under a kilometer of glacier. Locals name it for the slow chiming it makes when the ice groans; xenobiologists file it as a crystal-siphon.

A mature colony is a low dome two to four meters across, anchored by a fibrous holdfast that etches mineral tunnels into basalt. - **Filter feeding.** Cilia inside the tubes beat in coordinated waves, drawing water through a mucus net that traps bacteria, diatom-analogues, and organic snow. The net is rolled into the medullary cushions and digested extracellularly.
- **Chemosynthesis by symbionts.** Sulfur-oxidizing microbes live in the tube walls, fed by a trickle of vent fluid the holdfast wicks upward. They fix carbon; the host takes a share as sugars and amino acids. In return the colony keeps them in a stable redox gradient and shields them from oxygen spikes.
- **Light scavenging.** Near the ice–water interface, a faint blue glow leaks down. Outer tube walls contain stacked guanine-like platelets that act as a crude lens, focusing that light onto a thin band of photosynthetic symbionts. It is supplementary, not primary—enough to top up energy during the long polar “day,” not enough to live on.

Metabolism is slow. A colony may add only a few centimeters of tube a local year. Waste ammonia is vented through pores at the tube tips; excess silica is laid down as new wall, so growth and excretion are the same process.

There is no brain and no eyes in the animal sense. A nerve net times ciliary beats and tube posture. Three sensory modes matter:

- **Flow.** Hairs on tube rims detect shear. In a surge the crown folds, protecting the mucus nets.
- **Chemistry.** Dissolved sulfide, oxygen, and a specific peptide from wounded neighbors are all read by receptor patches in the cushions. High sulfide opens the holdfast’s wick; a wound-peptide triggers mineral plugging and a local halt in feeding.
- **Vibration.** The silica tubes ring at characteristic frequencies. Colonies within a few meters tune their tube lengths so their “voices” do not overlap—spacing that also keeps filter currents from stealing each other’s catch. The chiming humans hear is an incidental byproduct of this spacing behavior, amplified by the ice.

Most of the year the colony grows by budding new zooids from the medullary cushions—clonal, asexual, genetically identical. It is multicellular, heterotrophic at the host level, autotrophic only through partners, sessile as an adult, and clonal with an occasional sexual spore stage. It is not intelligent, not predatory, and not parasitic on large animals. Its ecological role is a slow reef-builder and a living filter: silica lattice, sulfur chemistry, and a patient net in cold water.

The creature is a **glass-moth**, a slow, colonial animal that lives in the mineral storms of a cold, dim world. Locals—if there were any—might call it a single beast. Biologically it is closer to a moving reef: one coordinated body made of many semi-independent modules.

### Habitat
The planet orbits a dull orange star under a permanent high haze. Light at the surface is about a twentieth of an Earth noon, and most energy arrives as infrared and as weak electrical charge from dust storms. The ground is a mix of basalt gravel, iron-oxide crust, and shallow brine pans that freeze and thaw on a long seasonal cycle. Glass-moths live on the windward faces of low ridges, where charged dust settles and the brine seeps up through cracks.

### Body plan
A mature colony is two to four meters across and only a few centimeters thick, shaped like a ragged umbrella pressed against the rock. The “skin” is not flesh in the Earth sense. It is a flexible lattice of silica spicules grown by the animal itself, bound by a protein–polysaccharide glue that stays pliable well below freezing. In strong light the lattice looks faintly translucent, which is where the name comes from; in ordinary conditions it is a dull amber-gray, dusted with red grit.

Under the lattice are hundreds of soft lobes, each about the size of a human palm. Every lobe has:

- a **feeding pad** that faces the rock or the brine film
- a **respiratory gallery** of fine tubes opening to the air
- a **nerve ring** connected to neighboring lobes by living cables
- a **storage bladder** filled with a thick, antifreeze-rich fluid

The lobes share one circulatory gel. There is no single heart. Waves of contraction pass through the gel, pushed by muscle-like fibers in the cables. Cut a lobe free and it can live for days, feeding and repairing itself, but it stops reproducing and eventually starves unless it rejoins a colony. So the organism is modular, not truly unicellular, and not a loose herd of separate animals either.

### Metabolism
Glass-moths are **chemo-mixotrophs**. They do not rely on sunlight the way plants do. Their main energy comes from oxidizing reduced iron and sulfur compounds that leach out of the rock, using oxygen when the brine is aerated and switching to nitrate or even iron itself as an electron acceptor when oxygen is scarce. A secondary system harvests tiny currents from wind-driven charged dust: mineral hairs on the upper lattice act like a crude rectifier, and the charge helps pump ions across membranes. Photosynthesis, if it can be called that, is minor—a few pigments capture red and near-infrared light to top up energy stores, not to build the body.

They “eat” by dissolving mineral crust and microbial films with organic acids and a set of enzymes that work in the cold, then absorbing the ions and small molecules through the feeding pad. Large prey is not part of their life. A passing smaller animal that settles on the lattice may be trapped by sticky threads and slowly digested at the surface, but that is scavenging, not hunting.

Their body fluids stay liquid at temperatures that would freeze Earth blood because they load them with small sugars and a family of charged peptides that disrupt ice crystals. Growth is slow: a colony might add one new lobe every few local weeks.

### Senses and behavior
There are no eyes. Light-sensitive cells in the lattice tell the colony when a dust wall is coming so it can flatten and seal its galleries. The real senses are chemical and electrical. Each lobe tastes the brine for metal ions and for the scent of other colonies. The mineral hairs also detect changes in the local electric field, which lets the animal feel approaching storms and the movement of anything that disturbs the charged dust.

Behavior is mostly postural. In calm weather the lattice lifts a little so air can move through the galleries. Before a storm it clamps down, vents stored gas, and sometimes releases a cloud of fine silica flakes that stick to neighboring rock—seed sites for later growth. Colonies avoid overlapping. When two meet, they exchange chemical signals through the brine; usually one withdraws its edge. If both are starving, they may fuse cables and become one larger colony, sorting their lobes over many days until the nerve pattern is unified. That fusion is slow and incomplete: scars in the lattice mark old mergers for years.

Reproduction is both budding and a kind of broadcast spawning. Most new lobes are clones budded at the rim. Once a season, when brine is deepest, mature lobes grow internal packets of genetic material wrapped in tough gel. These packets are not eggs in the familiar sense and not spores of a fungus; they are diploid propagules produced after a brief exchange of hereditary material between neighboring colonies through temporary bridges. The bridges look like pale threads and last only hours. After exchange, each colony packages mixed genomes into the packets and sheds them into the brine. Currents carry them downhill. A packet that lodges in a crack can found a new colony if iron, moisture, and a bit of oxygen are present. Most do not.

There are no separate sexes. Any mature colony can donate and receive hereditary material. Relatedness is tracked in the chemistry of the lattice: close kin fuse more readily; distant colonies repel.

### What kind of organism it is
In Earth terms it sits nearest to animals, not plants or fungi, but the fit is imperfect. It has differentiated tissues, a shared internal fluid, coordinated movement, and a nervous system that integrates information across modules. It is heterotrophic at its core, even though it also draws energy from minerals and a little light. It is colonial in the way some marine invertebrates are colonial: parts can survive alone, but the reproductive and behavioral whole is the colony.

It is not intelligent. Its “decisions” are thresholds—ion levels, charge, kinship chemicals—playing out as slow changes in shape. A glass-moth does not hunt, speak, or build. It weathers. On that dim ridge, weathering is enough.
